categories.title: Repository Bundles
categories.summary: Package a repository into a single file.

lessons.title: Bundle an Entire Repository
lessons.objective: Identify the command that packages every reference into one file.
lessons.scenario: You need to move a repository to a machine with no network access, using one file on a USB drive.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. git bundle create repo.bundle --all writes every reference into a single transferable file.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Use git bundle create repo.bundle --all to package the whole repository into one file.

lessons.title: Clean and Optimize a Repository
lessons.scenario: A local repository has grown large and needs object cleanup and storage optimization.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. git gc cleans unnecessary files and optimizes local repository storage.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Use git gc for repository cleanup and storage optimization.
lessons.safetyWarning: Review repository state and Git documentation before cleanup operations.

categories.title: Daily Git Workflow
categories.summary: The commands used in everyday work.

lessons.title: Undo a Commit and Keep the Changes Staged
lessons.objective: Distinguish a soft reset from a hard reset.
lessons.scenario: You committed too early. You want the commit undone but every change kept, still staged.
lessons.prompt: Which command undoes the commit without losing work?
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. git reset --soft HEAD~1 moves the branch back one commit and keeps the changes staged.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: git reset --soft HEAD~1 undoes the commit while keeping your changes staged.
lessons.safetyWarning: Rewriting history affects commits you may have shared. Confirm the branch is unpublished before resetting.

lessons.title: Discard a Commit and Its Changes
lessons.scenario: A commit and everything in it must be thrown away on a local branch you have never pushed.
lessons.prompt: Which command discards both the commit and its changes?
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. git reset --hard HEAD~1 removes the commit and the changes it contained.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: git reset --hard HEAD~1 is the form that also discards the changes. The soft form keeps them.
lessons.safetyWarning: This permanently discards uncommitted and committed work. There is no undo once the objects are pruned.

lessons.title: Discard Working Tree Changes
lessons.objective: Identify the command that restores tracked files.
lessons.scenario: Edits across the working tree are wrong and should return to the last commit, leaving the index alone.
lessons.prompt: Which command restores the working tree?
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. git restore . returns tracked files in the working tree to their committed state.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: git restore . restores the working tree. The --staged form unstages instead.

lessons.title: Unstage Everything
lessons.scenario: Files were staged by mistake. The edits must stay, but nothing should be staged.
lessons.prompt: Which command unstages without touching the edits?
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. git restore --staged . removes files from the index and leaves the working tree untouched.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: git restore --staged . unstages. Without --staged the command overwrites your edits instead.

lessons.title: Move to an Existing Branch
lessons.scenario: A branch already exists and you need to work on it.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. git switch branch-name moves to a branch that already exists.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: git switch branch-name switches to an existing branch. The -c form creates a new one.

lessons.title: Create and Move to a Branch
lessons.scenario: You are starting a feature and the branch does not exist yet.
lessons.prompt: Which command creates the branch and moves to it?
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. git switch -c feature/name creates the branch and switches to it.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: The -c option is what creates the branch: git switch -c feature/name.
